notes.front: In Nexus, who is a Nexus Integration Team Member?
notes.back: Someone on the Nexus Integration Team besides the Product Owner and Scrum Master, often a Scrum Team member, who helps teams adopt tools and practices.
notes.explanation: Such members help the Scrum Teams deliver a valuable, useful Integrated Increment that frequently meets the Definition of Done.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: The Nexus Integration Team often consists of Scrum Team members who help the Scrum Teams to adopt tools and practices that contribute to the Scrum Teams’ ability to deliver a valuable and useful Integrated Increment that frequently meets the Definition of Done.
notes.example: Like a tester from one Scrum Team who also spends part of each Sprint helping every team in the Nexus adopt a shared automated test suite.

notes.front: What is Nexus Sprint Planning?
notes.back: The Nexus event that coordinates the activities of all Scrum Teams in a Nexus for a single Sprint.
notes.explanation: Appropriate representatives from each Scrum Team meet with the Product Owner to plan the Sprint.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Planning”, p. 7
notes.evidence: The purpose of Nexus Sprint Planning is to coordinate the activities of all Scrum Teams within a Nexus for a single Sprint. Appropriate representatives from each Scrum Team and the Product Owner meet to plan the Sprint.
notes.example: Like Sprint Planning, but the people in the room are representatives of several Scrum Teams plus their one Product Owner, planning one shared Sprint.

notes.front: What is the Nexus Daily Scrum?
notes.back: A Nexus event where representatives of the Scrum Teams identify integration issues and inspect progress toward the Nexus Sprint Goal.
notes.explanation: They inspect the current state of the integrated Increment and look for newly discovered cross-team dependencies or impacts.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Daily Scrum”, p. 8
notes.evidence: The purpose of the Nexus Daily Scrum is to identify any integration issues and inspect progress toward the Nexus Sprint Goal. Appropriate representatives from the Scrum Teams attend the Nexus Daily Scrum, inspect the current state of the integrated Increment, and identify integration issues and newly discovered cross-team dependencies or impacts.
notes.example: Like a Daily Scrum, but held by a few people from each of several teams, and centred on how their combined work fits together.

notes.front: What is the Nexus Sprint Review?
notes.back: The event at the end of the Sprint that gathers feedback on the Nexus’s done Integrated Increment and determines future adaptations.
notes.explanation: It plays the part of a Sprint Review, but its subject is the combined work of every Scrum Team in the Nexus.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Review”, p. 8
notes.evidence: The Nexus Sprint Review is held at the end of the Sprint to provide feedback on the done Integrated Increment that the Nexus has built over the Sprint and determine future adaptations.
notes.example: Like a Sprint Review, but stakeholders give feedback on the integrated work of all the Nexus’s teams together.

notes.front: What is the purpose of the Nexus Sprint Retrospective?
notes.back: To plan ways to increase quality and effectiveness across the whole Nexus.
notes.explanation: It lifts the Sprint Retrospective’s aim from one Scrum Team to the whole group of teams.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Retrospective”, p. 8
notes.evidence: The purpose of the Nexus Sprint Retrospective is to plan ways to increase quality and effectiveness across the whole Nexus.
notes.example: Like a Sprint Retrospective, but it tackles problems that cross team boundaries, such as a test environment every team shares.

notes.front: What is a Nexus Sprint Backlog?
notes.back: The composite of the Nexus Sprint Goal and the Product Backlog items from the individual Scrum Teams’ Sprint Backlogs.
notes.explanation: It is used to highlight dependencies and the flow of work during the Sprint.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Backlog”, p. 9
notes.evidence: A Nexus Sprint Backlog is the composite of the Nexus Sprint Goal and Product Backlog items from the Sprint Backlogs of the individual Scrum Teams. It is used to highlight dependencies and the flow of work during the Sprint.
notes.example: Like a Sprint Backlog, but it spans several teams and shows, for instance, that one team’s item waits on another team’s.

notes.front: What is the Nexus Sprint Goal?
notes.back: The single objective for the Nexus in a Sprint, and the commitment for the Nexus Sprint Backlog.
notes.explanation: It is the sum of all the work and Sprint Goals of the Scrum Teams within the Nexus.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Commitment: Nexus Sprint Goal”, p. 9
notes.evidence: The commitment for the Nexus Sprint Backlog is the Nexus Sprint Goal. The Nexus Sprint Goal is a single objective for the Nexus. It is the sum of all the work and Sprint Goals of the Scrum Teams within the Nexus.
notes.example: Like a Sprint Goal, but one objective shared by all teams, such as “shoppers can return an order online”, which each team’s own goal serves.

notes.front: Does Nexus change Scrum’s core design, leave out elements or negate its rules?
notes.back: No. Scaled Scrum is still Scrum.
notes.explanation: The guide warns that changing or dropping parts covers up problems and limits Scrum’s benefits, potentially even rendering it useless.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Purpose of the Nexus Guide”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Scaled Scrum is still Scrum. Nexus does not change the core design or ideas of Scrum, or leave out elements, or negate the rules of Scrum. Doing so covers up problems and limits the benefits of Scrum, potentially even rendering it useless.

notes.front: A Sprint in Nexus is {{c1::the same as in Scrum}}; the Scrum Teams in a Nexus produce a single Integrated Increment.
notes.back: the same as in Scrum
notes.explanation: The Scrum Teams’ work comes together in one Integrated Increment, not a separate Increment per team.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “The Sprint”, p. 7
notes.evidence: A Sprint in Nexus is the same as in Scrum. The Scrum Teams in a Nexus produce a single Integrated Increment.

notes.front: Nexus minimally extends the Scrum framework only where {{c1::absolutely necessary}} to let multiple teams work from a single Product Backlog.
notes.back: absolutely necessary
notes.explanation: Its extensions exist so that several teams can build one Integrated Increment that meets a goal.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Definition”, p. 4
notes.evidence: It minimally extends the Scrum framework only where absolutely necessary to enable multiple teams to work from a single Product Backlog to build an Integrated Increment that meets a goal.

notes.front: In Nexus theory, which mismatch concerns how far different concerns are independently separated in the product?
notes.back: Product structure.
notes.explanation: That degree of separation greatly affects how complex it is to create an integrated product release.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Theory”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Product structure: The degree to which different concerns are independently separated in the product will greatly affect the complexity of creating an integrated product release.

notes.front: In Nexus theory, which mismatch concerns the way people communicate within and between teams?
notes.back: Communication structure.
notes.explanation: Delays in communication and feedback reduce the flow of work.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Theory”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Communication structure: The way that people communicate within and between teams affects their ability to get work done; delays in communication and feedback reduce the flow of work.

notes.front: When more people add complexity and dependencies, what practice does the Nexus Guide say can be important in delivering more value?
notes.back: Scaling down: reducing the number of people who work on something.
notes.explanation: More people and a bigger product increase complexity, dependencies, the need for collaboration and the number of communication pathways in decisions.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Theory”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Increasing the number of people and the size of a product increases complexity and dependencies, the need for collaboration, and the number of communication pathways involved in making decisions. Scaling-down, reducing the number of people who work on something, can be an important practice in delivering more value.

notes.front: The figure shows the Nexus framework. In a Nexus, do the Scrum Teams still address integration issues, or does the Nexus Integration Team take them over?
notes.back: The Scrum Teams still address them; the Nexus Integration Team provides a focal point of integration.
notes.explanation: In the figure the Nexus Integration Team sits beside the ring of Scrum Teams, joined by a two-way arrow: it focuses integration work without removing it from the teams.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: While Scrum Teams address integration issues within the Nexus, the Nexus Integration Team provides a focal point of integration for the Nexus.

image.alt: The Nexus framework as a flow from left to right. A Product Backlog, with a looping arrow labelled Cross-Team Refinement, feeds Nexus Sprint Planning, which produces the Nexus Sprint Backlog. That flows into a large ring labelled 3-9 Scrum Teams, holding several teams around a triangle marked Integrated Work. Beside the ring are the Nexus Integration Team, joined to it by a two-way arrow, and the Nexus Daily Scrum with the teams’ Daily Scrums. The ring feeds the Integrated Increment, then the Nexus Sprint Review. Arrows return from the Nexus Sprint Review to the Product Backlog and, through the Nexus Sprint Retrospective, to Nexus Sprint Planning.
image.credit: Scrum.org, The Nexus Guide (January 2021), Figure 1: The Nexus Framework, p. 5

notes.front: What does integration include in Nexus, and what should the Nexus Integration Team use to resolve it?
notes.back: Technical and non-technical cross-functional team constraints; it should use bottom-up intelligence from within the Nexus.
notes.explanation: These are constraints that may impede the Nexus’s ability to deliver a constantly Integrated Increment.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Integration includes addressing technical and non-technical cross-functional team constraints that may impede a Nexus’ ability to deliver a constantly Integrated Increment. It should use bottom-up intelligence from within the Nexus to achieve resolution.

notes.front: Is the membership of the Nexus Integration Team fixed?
notes.back: No. Its composition may change over time to reflect the current needs of the Nexus.
notes.explanation: Appropriate members are the people with the skills and knowledge to help resolve the issues the Nexus faces at that point in time.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Appropriate members are the people with the necessary skills and knowledge to help resolve the issues the Nexus faces at any point in time. Composition of the Nexus Integration Team may change over time to reflect the current needs of a Nexus.

notes.front: What is the Nexus Integration Team responsible for coaching and guiding the Scrum Teams to do?
notes.back: Acquire, implement and learn practices and tools that improve their ability to produce a valuable, useful Increment.
notes.explanation: Coaching and guiding leaves the teams as the ones who acquire, implement and learn the practices.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: The Nexus Integration Team is responsible for coaching and guiding the Scrum Teams to acquire, implement, and learn practices and tools that improve their ability to produce a valuable, useful Increment.

notes.front: What is the Scrum Master on the Nexus Integration Team accountable for?
notes.back: Ensuring the Nexus framework is understood and enacted as described in the Nexus Guide.
notes.explanation: This mirrors a Scrum Master’s accountability for Scrum, applied to the Nexus framework.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: The Scrum Master in the Nexus Integration Team is accountable for ensuring the Nexus framework is understood and enacted as described in the Nexus Guide.

notes.front: May the Nexus Integration Team’s Scrum Master also be a Scrum Master of Scrum Teams in the Nexus?
notes.back: Yes, of one or more of them.
notes.explanation: The guide permits this double role; it does not require it.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: This Scrum Master may also be a Scrum Master in one or more of the Scrum Teams in the Nexus.

notes.front: Which comes first for a person on both: Nexus Integration Team membership or Scrum Team membership?
notes.back: Nexus Integration Team membership takes precedence.
notes.explanation: Once their Nexus Integration Team responsibility is satisfied, they can work as members of their own Scrum Teams.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Membership in the Nexus Integration Team takes precedence over individual Scrum Team membership. As long as their Nexus Integration Team responsibility is satisfied, they can work as team members of their respective Scrum Teams.

notes.front: The precedence of Nexus Integration Team membership helps ensure that the work to resolve issues affecting {{c1::multiple teams}} has priority.
notes.back: multiple teams
notes.explanation: The Nexus Guide gives this as the purpose of the precedence rule.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: This preference helps ensure that the work to resolve issues affecting multiple teams has priority.

notes.front: Except where noted, who attends Nexus events?
notes.back: Whichever members of the Nexus are needed to achieve the event’s intended outcome most effectively.
notes.explanation: At scale, it may not be practical for every member of the Nexus to take part.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Events”, p. 7
notes.evidence: At scale, it may not be practical for all members of the Nexus to participate to share information or to come to an agreement. Except where noted, Nexus events are attended by whichever members of the Nexus are needed to achieve the intended outcome of the event most effectively.

notes.front: What does an adequately refined Product Backlog minimise during Nexus Sprint Planning?
notes.back: The emergence of new dependencies.
notes.explanation: It links refinement done before the event, by each team and across teams, to a smoother Nexus Sprint Planning.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Cross-Team Refinement”, p. 7
notes.evidence: An adequately refined Product Backlog will minimize the emergence of new dependencies during Nexus Sprint Planning.

notes.front: Does Cross-Team Refinement replace each Scrum Team’s own refinement?
notes.back: No. Where needed, each team continues its own refinement so items are ready for Nexus Sprint Planning.
notes.explanation: Cross-Team Refinement adds to the teams’ own refinement rather than replacing it.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Cross-Team Refinement”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Where needed, each Scrum Team will continue their own refinement in order for the Product Backlog items to be ready for selection in a Nexus Sprint Planning event.

notes.front: Which result of Nexus Sprint Planning aligns with the Product Goal and describes the purpose the whole Nexus will achieve in the Sprint?
notes.back: The Nexus Sprint Goal.
notes.explanation: It links the long-term Product Goal to the Sprint, and each team’s Sprint Goal then aligns with it.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Planning”, p. 7
notes.evidence: a Nexus Sprint Goal that aligns with the Product Goal and describes the purpose that will be achieved by the Nexus during the Sprint

notes.front: Which result of Nexus Sprint Planning gives each Scrum Team its own objective aligned with the Nexus Sprint Goal?
notes.back: A Sprint Goal for each Scrum Team.
notes.explanation: Teams keep their own Sprint Goals in a Nexus; these align with the shared Nexus Sprint Goal.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Planning”, p. 7
notes.evidence: a Sprint Goal for each Scrum Team that aligns with the Nexus Sprint Goal

notes.front: Which single result of Nexus Sprint Planning represents the Nexus’s work toward the Nexus Sprint Goal and makes cross-team dependencies transparent?
notes.back: A single Nexus Sprint Backlog.
notes.explanation: There is one for the whole Nexus, alongside the teams’ own Sprint Backlogs.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Planning”, p. 7
notes.evidence: a single Nexus Sprint Backlog that represents the work of the Nexus toward the Nexus Sprint Goal and makes cross-team dependencies transparent

notes.front: Which result of Nexus Sprint Planning makes transparent the work each Scrum Team will do in support of the Nexus Sprint Goal?
notes.back: A Sprint Backlog for each Scrum Team.
notes.explanation: Each team’s own plan stays visible and points at the shared goal.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Planning”, p. 7
notes.evidence: A Sprint Backlog for each Scrum Team, which makes transparent the work they will do in support of the Nexus Sprint Goal

notes.front: How does each Scrum Team’s Daily Scrum complement the Nexus Daily Scrum?
notes.back: It creates the team’s plan for the day, focused mainly on the integration issues raised at the Nexus Daily Scrum.
notes.explanation: So team Daily Scrums still happen in a Nexus, and they pick up what the Nexus Daily Scrum surfaced.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Daily Scrum”, p. 8
notes.evidence: Each Scrum Team’s Daily Scrum complements the Nexus Daily Scrum by creating plans for the day, focused primarily on addressing the integration issues raised during the Nexus Daily Scrum.

notes.front: Is the Nexus Daily Scrum the only time Scrum Teams in a Nexus may adjust their plan?
notes.back: No. Cross-team communication can happen throughout the day to adapt or re-plan the rest of the Sprint’s work.
notes.explanation: The Nexus Daily Scrum is a fixed point for inspection, not a gate on re-planning.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Daily Scrum”, p. 8
notes.evidence: The Nexus Daily Scrum is not the only time Scrum Teams in the Nexus are allowed to adjust their plan. Cross-team communication can occur throughout the day for more detailed discussions about adapting or re-planning the rest of the Sprint’s work.

notes.front: How does the Nexus Daily Scrum differ from a Scrum Team’s Daily Scrum?
notes.back: The Nexus Daily Scrum identifies integration issues across teams; each team’s Daily Scrum then plans its day around those issues.
notes.explanation: Both still happen in a Nexus: the Nexus-level event surfaces the integration issues and the team-level one plans how to act on them.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Daily Scrum”, p. 8
notes.evidence: inspect the current state of the integrated Increment, and identify integration issues and newly discovered cross-team dependencies or impacts. Each Scrum Team’s Daily Scrum complements the Nexus Daily Scrum by creating plans for the day, focused primarily on addressing the integration issues raised during the Nexus Daily Scrum.

notes.front: In a Nexus, does each Scrum Team still hold its own Sprint Review?
notes.back: No. The Nexus Sprint Review replaces individual Scrum Team Sprint Reviews.
notes.explanation: Stakeholder feedback is captured on the entire Integrated Increment, not on each team’s part.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Review”, p. 8
notes.evidence: Since the entire Integrated Increment is the focus for capturing feedback from stakeholders, a Nexus Sprint Review replaces individual Scrum Team Sprint Reviews.

notes.front: What are two things the Nexus inspects at the Nexus Sprint Retrospective about how the last Sprint went?
notes.back: Any two of: individuals, teams, interactions, processes, tools, its Definition of Done.
notes.explanation: The inspection covers the whole Nexus, so the teams themselves are among the things examined.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Retrospective”, p. 8
notes.evidence: The Nexus inspects how the last Sprint went with regards to individuals, teams, interactions, processes, tools, and its Definition of Done.

notes.front: In a Nexus, what do the Scrum Teams’ own Sprint Retrospectives add to the Nexus Sprint Retrospective?
notes.back: Besides their own team improvements, they use bottom-up intelligence to focus on issues that affect the whole Nexus.
notes.explanation: So team Retrospectives still happen in a Nexus, unlike team Sprint Reviews.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Retrospective”, p. 8
notes.evidence: In addition to individual team improvements, the Scrum Teams’ Sprint Retrospectives complement the Nexus Sprint Retrospective by using bottom-up intelligence to focus on issues that affect the Nexus as a whole.

notes.front: In a Nexus, the {{c1::Nexus Sprint Retrospective}} concludes the Sprint.
notes.back: Nexus Sprint Retrospective
notes.explanation: It takes the closing place that the Sprint Retrospective has for a single Scrum Team.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Retrospective”, p. 8
notes.evidence: The Nexus Sprint Retrospective concludes the Sprint.

notes.front: What does the Nexus Sprint Goal encourage the Scrum Teams in a Nexus to do?
notes.back: Work together rather than on separate initiatives, giving the Nexus coherence and focus for the Sprint.
notes.explanation: It is created at Nexus Sprint Planning, and teams keep it in mind as they work during the Sprint.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Commitment: Nexus Sprint Goal”, p. 9
notes.evidence: It creates coherence and focus for the Nexus for the Sprint by encouraging the Scrum Teams to work together rather than on separate initiatives. The Nexus Sprint Goal is created at the Nexus Sprint Planning event and added to the Nexus Sprint Backlog. As Scrum Teams work during the Sprint, they keep the Nexus Sprint Goal in mind.

notes.front: May a Scrum Team in a Nexus apply its own Definition of Done?
notes.back: Yes, a more stringent one, but never less rigorous criteria than those agreed for the Integrated Increment.
notes.explanation: The agreed Definition of Done works as a floor for every team, not a ceiling.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Commitment: Definition of Done”, p. 10
notes.evidence: They may choose to apply a more stringent Definition of Done within their own teams, but cannot apply less rigorous criteria than agreed for the Integrated Increment.

notes.front: Why does artifact transparency matter even more in a Nexus?
notes.back: Decisions are only as effective as artifact transparency, and flawed decisions’ impact can be magnified at the scale of Nexus.
notes.explanation: Incomplete or partial information leads to incorrect or flawed decisions.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Commitment: Definition of Done”, p. 10
notes.evidence: Decisions made based on the state of artifacts are only as effective as the level of artifact transparency. Incomplete or partial information will lead to incorrect or flawed decisions. The impact of those decisions can be magnified at the scale of Nexus.

notes.front: Can you implement only parts of Nexus and still call it Nexus?
notes.back: No. Implementing only parts is possible, but the result is not Nexus.
notes.explanation: As with Scrum, Nexus’s accountabilities, artifacts, events and rules are immutable.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “End Note”, p. 10
notes.evidence: As with the Scrum framework, the accountabilities in Nexus, its artifacts, events, and rules are immutable. Although implementing only parts of Nexus is possible, the result is not Nexus.

notes.front: Five Scrum Teams have just formed a Nexus. A programme manager tells the Scrum Master that the teams can now drop their own Daily Scrums, because “scaled Scrum works differently”. What should the Scrum Master say?
notes.back: A) Nexus does not leave out Scrum’s elements: scaled Scrum is still Scrum, so the teams keep their Daily Scrums
notes.explanation: Nexus does not leave out elements of Scrum. Its events replace a Scrum event only where the Nexus Guide says so, and it keeps each team’s Daily Scrum alongside the Nexus Daily Scrum.
notes.choices:
A) Nexus does not leave out Scrum’s elements: scaled Scrum is still Scrum, so the teams keep their Daily Scrums
B) Agree, because the Nexus Daily Scrum replaces the teams’ Daily Scrums
C) Agree for teams with few integration issues and keep them for the rest
D) Ask the Nexus Integration Team to decide which Scrum events each team keeps
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: each team’s Daily Scrum complements the Nexus Daily Scrum. C and D drop an event the Nexus Guide keeps; Nexus replaces a Scrum event only where its Guide says so, as with team Sprint Reviews.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Purpose of the Nexus Guide”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Scaled Scrum is still Scrum. Nexus does not change the core design or ideas of Scrum, or leave out elements, or negate the rules of Scrum. Doing so covers up problems and limits the benefits of Scrum, potentially even rendering it useless.

notes.front: An organisation starting Nexus asks its Scrum Master to design a set of new roles, sign-off stages and reporting layers “to make scaling safe”. What does the Nexus Guide suggest as the starting point?
notes.back: D) Build on Scrum and extend it only where absolutely necessary for several teams to work from one Product Backlog on one Integrated Increment
notes.explanation: Nexus builds on Scrum’s foundation and extends it minimally, only as far as multiple teams need to share one Product Backlog and build one Integrated Increment.
notes.choices:
A) Design the extra roles first and add Scrum later, once the structure is stable
B) Let each team choose its own framework and integrate the results at the end of the release
C) Replace the Product Owner with a committee so that each team is represented
D) Build on Scrum and extend it only where absolutely necessary for several teams to work from one Product Backlog on one Integrated Increment
notes.choicesExplained: A puts new structure ahead of Scrum, which Nexus builds on. C breaks the single Product Owner. B gives up the single Integrated Increment that Nexus exists to produce.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Definition”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Nexus builds upon Scrum’s foundation, and its parts will be familiar to those who have used Scrum. It minimally extends the Scrum framework only where absolutely necessary to enable multiple teams to work from a single Product Backlog to build an Integrated Increment that meets a goal.

notes.front: In a Nexus, two teams block each other every Sprint because almost every feature touches one tightly coupled billing module. Which mismatch named in the Nexus Guide is most at work?
notes.back: D) Product structure
notes.explanation: The problem lies in how poorly the product’s concerns are separated, which is what product structure describes.
notes.choices:
A) Communication structure
B) Team size
C) Sprint length
D) Product structure
notes.choicesExplained: A is about how people talk within and between teams, not how the product is built. B and C are not among the two mismatches the guide names.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Theory”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Product structure: The degree to which different concerns are independently separated in the product will greatly affect the complexity of creating an integrated product release.

notes.front: A Nexus of seven Scrum Teams finishes less each Sprint as cross-team dependencies grow. Management wants to add two more teams to catch up. What should the Scrum Master put forward?
notes.back: D) Consider scaling down: fewer people can deliver more value, since more people add complexity and dependencies
notes.explanation: The Nexus Guide says adding people increases complexity, dependencies and communication pathways, and that scaling down can deliver more value.
notes.choices:
A) Add the teams at once, since a Nexus may have up to about nine
B) Lengthen the Sprint so that the new teams have time to integrate
C) Let each team hold its own Sprint Review so that progress looks clearer
D) Consider scaling down: fewer people can deliver more value, since more people add complexity and dependencies
notes.choicesExplained: A treats the size limit as a target and ignores the dependency problem. B and C do not reduce dependencies, and C breaks the rule that the Nexus Sprint Review replaces team reviews.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Theory”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Increasing the number of people and the size of a product increases complexity and dependencies, the need for collaboration, and the number of communication pathways involved in making decisions. Scaling-down, reducing the number of people who work on something, can be an important practice in delivering more value.

notes.front: Each team in a Nexus says “our part is done”, but nobody combines the work, and integration fails at the end of every Sprint. Who is accountable for ensuring a done Integrated Increment is produced?
notes.back: A) The Nexus Integration Team
notes.explanation: The Nexus Guide gives the Nexus Integration Team this accountability for the combined work of the Nexus.
notes.choices:
A) The Nexus Integration Team
B) Each team’s Scrum Master, for that team’s part
C) The Developers of whichever team finishes last
D) The stakeholders at the Nexus Sprint Review
notes.choicesExplained: B and C split the combined result into team parts, which leaves no one accountable for the whole. D confuses giving feedback with accountability for producing the Increment.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 5
notes.evidence: The Nexus Integration Team is accountable for ensuring that a done Integrated Increment (the combined work completed by a Nexus) is produced at least once a Sprint.

notes.front: You are the Scrum Master on a Nexus Integration Team. Several teams still hold their own Sprint Reviews and skip the Nexus Daily Scrum. What is your accountability here?
notes.back: D) Ensure the Nexus framework is understood and enacted as the Nexus Guide describes
notes.explanation: This accountability sits with the Scrum Master on the Nexus Integration Team.
notes.choices:
A) Report the teams to their line managers
B) Leave it to the Product Owner, who has the final say
C) Accept it, because the teams are self-managing
D) Ensure the Nexus framework is understood and enacted as the Nexus Guide describes
notes.choicesExplained: A replaces coaching with escalation. C confuses self-management with dropping the framework. B: the Product Owner has the final say on the Product Backlog, not on how Nexus is enacted.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: The Scrum Master in the Nexus Integration Team is accountable for ensuring the Nexus framework is understood and enacted as described in the Nexus Guide.

notes.front: A Developer sits on both her Scrum Team and the Nexus Integration Team. Her team asks her to spend the whole Sprint on its own items, while a cross-team build failure is blocking three teams. What should come first?
notes.back: C) The cross-team build failure, because Nexus Integration Team membership takes precedence
notes.explanation: The Nexus Guide gives Nexus Integration Team membership precedence so that issues affecting multiple teams get priority.
notes.choices:
A) Her own team’s items, because she is a Developer there first
B) Whatever her own team’s Scrum Master decides
C) The cross-team build failure, because Nexus Integration Team membership takes precedence
D) Splitting her time equally, whatever the state of the build
notes.choicesExplained: A reverses the precedence rule. B hands the choice to one team although the issue affects several. D ignores that cross-team work is meant to have priority.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Integration Team”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Membership in the Nexus Integration Team takes precedence over individual Scrum Team membership. As long as their Nexus Integration Team responsibility is satisfied, they can work as team members of their respective Scrum Teams. This preference helps ensure that the work to resolve issues affecting multiple teams has priority.

notes.front: Nexus Sprint Planning ends with a Nexus Sprint Goal and a Nexus Sprint Backlog, but the teams leave without goals or plans of their own. What is still missing from the results of Nexus Sprint Planning?
notes.back: D) A Sprint Goal and a Sprint Backlog for each Scrum Team
notes.explanation: The Nexus Guide lists four results, two of them per team: a Sprint Goal and a Sprint Backlog for each Scrum Team.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: team goals and plans are optional in a Nexus
B) A separate Product Backlog for each team
C) A Definition of Done for each Sprint
D) A Sprint Goal and a Sprint Backlog for each Scrum Team
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: both are listed results. B breaks the single Product Backlog. C: the Definition of Done is the Increment’s commitment, not a planning result.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Planning”, p. 7
notes.evidence: a Sprint Goal for each Scrum Team that aligns with the Nexus Sprint Goal ● a single Nexus Sprint Backlog that represents the work of the Nexus toward the Nexus Sprint Goal and makes cross-team dependencies transparent ● A Sprint Backlog for each Scrum Team

notes.front: One team in a Nexus wants to hold its own Sprint Review with “its” stakeholders, as well as the Nexus Sprint Review. How should the Scrum Master respond?
notes.back: B) Explain that the Nexus Sprint Review replaces team Sprint Reviews, because feedback is sought on the whole Integrated Increment
notes.explanation: Feedback in a Nexus is captured on the entire Integrated Increment, so team reviews are replaced.
notes.choices:
A) Allow both, since more feedback is always better
B) Explain that the Nexus Sprint Review replaces team Sprint Reviews, because feedback is sought on the whole Integrated Increment
C) Replace the Nexus Sprint Review with one review per team
D) Hold the Nexus Sprint Review only in Sprints when integration succeeds
notes.choicesExplained: A and C bring back the team reviews that the Nexus Sprint Review replaces. D skips the event that inspects the Integrated Increment.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Nexus Sprint Review”, p. 8
notes.evidence: Since the entire Integrated Increment is the focus for capturing feedback from stakeholders, a Nexus Sprint Review replaces individual Scrum Team Sprint Reviews.

notes.front: Mid-Sprint, two teams in a Nexus each chase their own Sprint Goal and ignore a shared objective that needs both of them. Which Nexus element exists to counter this?
notes.back: A) The Nexus Sprint Goal
notes.explanation: The Nexus Guide says the Nexus Sprint Goal encourages teams to work together rather than on separate initiatives.
notes.choices:
A) The Nexus Sprint Goal
B) The Definition of Done for the Integrated Increment
C) Cross-Team Refinement
D) The Nexus Sprint Retrospective
notes.choicesExplained: B sets quality, not a shared objective. C forecasts which team will deliver which items and finds dependencies; it sets no objective. D inspects the Sprint at its end, too late to steer teams mid-Sprint.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Commitment: Nexus Sprint Goal”, p. 9
notes.evidence: It creates coherence and focus for the Nexus for the Sprint by encouraging the Scrum Teams to work together rather than on separate initiatives.

notes.front: Each team in a new Nexus wrote its own Definition of Done, and none of them mention integration. Who is responsible for a Definition of Done that applies to the Integrated Increment?
notes.back: B) The Nexus Integration Team
notes.explanation: The Nexus Integration Team is responsible for it, and every team must then define and adhere to it.
notes.choices:
A) Each team separately, as now
B) The Nexus Integration Team
C) The stakeholders who attend the Nexus Sprint Review
D) The Scrum Master of the largest team
notes.choicesExplained: A leaves the combined work without a shared standard. C and D name people the Nexus Guide does not give this responsibility.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Commitment: Definition of Done”, p. 9
notes.evidence: The Nexus Integration Team is responsible for a Definition of Done that can be applied to the Integrated Increment developed each Sprint. All Scrum Teams within the Nexus must define and adhere to this Definition of Done.

notes.front: In a Nexus, one team wants to skip the performance tests the agreed Definition of Done requires, to meet a date. Another team wants to add extra security reviews to its own Definition of Done. As Scrum Master, which do you support?
notes.back: C) Only the extra security reviews
notes.explanation: A team may be more stringent than the agreed Definition of Done but may not be less rigorous.
notes.choices:
A) Both, since each team is self-managing
B) Neither, since every team must use exactly the agreed wording
C) Only the extra security reviews
D) Only the skipped performance tests, since dates matter to stakeholders
notes.choicesExplained: A and D accept criteria less rigorous than those agreed for the Integrated Increment. B forbids the stricter team Definition of Done that the guide allows.
notes.source: The Nexus Guide (January 2021), “Commitment: Definition of Done”, p. 10
notes.evidence: They may choose to apply a more stringent Definition of Done within their own teams, but cannot apply less rigorous criteria than agreed for the Integrated Increment.
